not_for: text the user wrote in their own voice (their sample wins)
strengths: content gate with each rule traced to a numbered table of the IdeaLens study (arXiv 2610.06778)
six rules have a mechanical or flag-and-judge check; offline, stdlib, 42 tests; reviewed hits can be recorded with an ok marker or --allow
refuses to invent specifics: missing material becomes a question for the author
separate EN and ES word lists; allows verified absolutes and stated conditions
stop-slop and ux-copy stay installed and untouched
weaknesses: evidence is one author-run preprint, features rated by language models, never replicated
the study reads English long-form text of 500+ words; short strings are out of range
Spanish word lists are UNREVIEWED; no Spanish human-follows-AI-plan test exists
lint is regex and only a floor: it misses "cannot", "may" and filler; H4 and H11 are noisy on technical docs; every hit needs a person
under a no-new-facts rule layer 1 mostly yields questions for the author, so little text changes (comparison: 3 small edits across 2 texts, none on UI strings)
J rules (H3, H7, H10, H12, H13) have no mechanical check
when_selector_picks: job is writing or reviewing long public or user-facing prose (README, wiki, release note, landing, store copy, post) in English or Spanish. Selector rule: prose -> budgit-humanize first (content gate, then layer 2); UI strings of a few words -> design:ux-copy first, humanize only with --kind ui. Both may run on one job; stop-slop stays installed and untouched. Never for legal or security wording.
